issues.description: The study reconstructs past events and then analyzes already-existing texts, so it is retrospective. Calling this a prospective design is conceptually incorrect and can mislead readers about temporal prediction and causal/predictive validity.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt, overcoming the power issues of a ‘true’ prospective study design.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames the work as identifying suicide risk in real time, but no real-time monitoring, prospective follow-up, alerting, or out-of-sample prediction was performed. Retrospective association within selected historical windows cannot establish real-time clinical utility.
issues.quote: we aimed to improve our ability to assess suicide risk dynamically in real time.

issues.description: The term biomarker implies validated, reliable indicators with demonstrated diagnostic or prognostic value. The study is a small retrospective pilot with exploratory analyses and no prospective validation, so referring to the findings as biomarkers overstates the evidence.
issues.quote: In this study, we aimed to utilize ecological private SMS data to gain insight into possible novel, real-time digital biomarkers of suicidal behaviors.

issues.description: The analytic sample is very small for a multilevel design with many outcomes, interactions, pairwise contrasts, and random effects. This increases instability of estimates, Type I error risk, Type II error risk, and poor generalizability.
issues.quote: A sample of 33 participants with at least one reported past suicide attempt were recruited from the Charlottesville community.

issues.description: The sample is demographically narrow, mostly female, White, college-aged, and from one community. Suicide risk, communication patterns, platform use, and lethality differ by age, gender, race/ethnicity, and clinical setting, so findings may not generalize to broader high-risk populations.
issues.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

issues.description: Participants at high or imminent current suicide risk were excluded. This limits applicability to the very population for whom real-time imminent-risk detection would be clinically most important.
issues.quote: Any participants with intense thoughts of suicide who were determined to be at “high risk” or “imminent risk” for suicidal behavior (as determined by a suicide risk assessment instrument) were excluded from study participation and referred for clinical care.

issues.subcategory: eligibility required accessible historical digital data
issues.description: Requiring access to historical messaging data creates a selected sample of people with compatible devices, retained messages, and recoverable data. This may systematically exclude people with older attempts, deleted messages, privacy settings, lower socioeconomic resources, different phone habits, or different clinical profiles.
issues.quote: Inclusion criteria included: (1) confirmation of group status based on report of past suicide attempt; (2) adult status (≥18 years-old); (3) availability of and access to personal messaging data dating back prior to significant life events (e.g., suicide attempt); and (4) minimal or no current desire to die

issues.description: Only a subset of reported episodes had SMS data. Missingness is likely nonrandom because it depends on device type, encryption, backups, age of episode, deletion behavior, and communication habits. Mixed models do not solve bias from nonrandom missingness.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.description: The manuscript documents systematic technical barriers to retrieving text data, particularly for some iPhone users. This can bias the analytic dataset and reduce replicability unless missingness mechanisms and excluded cases are characterized.
issues.quote: Though most text data was successfully extracted from both Android and iPhone devices, a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data.

issues.description: The study depended on participants' current and old devices/backups, but recovery of older or cloud-stored messages was often unsuccessful. This threatens completeness of exposure measurement, especially for older suicide attempts.
issues.quote: Though participants were generally interested in providing as much information as possible, efforts to collection additional messages outside of their current mobile device were minimally successful.

issues.description: The primary high-risk outcome combines actual attempts, interrupted attempts, aborted attempts, and events with no enacted physical attempt. These phenomena may differ substantially in intent, capability, planning, lethality, and proximal dynamics, so combining them may dilute or distort markers of suicide attempts.
issues.quote: reported ‘suicide attempts’ also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than ‘suicide ideation’ so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions.

issues.subcategory: low physical lethality of attempt episodes
issues.description: Most incidents classified as attempts caused no physical harm. Findings may therefore reflect aborted planning/high ideation rather than behavioral suicide attempts, limiting inference about medically serious attempts or deaths.
issues.quote: Based on participants’ description of the objective lethality of the attempt, 29% of incidents involved some action being taken in which some physical harm was caused ... while 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm

issues.description: Episode type depended heavily on participants' retrospective interpretations. Without independent clinical adjudication or medical record verification, misclassification between ideation, aborted attempt, interrupted attempt, and actual attempt is likely and can bias within-person contrasts.
issues.quote: classification of episode type depended on participants’ interpretations of whether their behaviors qualified as a specific type of event.

issues.description: The manuscript gives conflicting descriptions of the attempt episode window: one week prior to attempt, two-week episodes, and models using days -14 to 0. This ambiguity impairs reproducibility and interpretation of temporal slopes.
issues.quote: past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”;

issues.description: A two-week window is described, but the time variable ranges from -14 to 0, which includes 15 calendar days if both endpoints are included. It is also unclear whether the attempt day itself was included, which matters because communications on the attempt day may differ from preceding risk escalation.
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)

issues.description: The optimal window was partly assessed by visual inspection of the same data and variables later analyzed. This introduces circularity and researcher degrees of freedom, increasing the chance of capitalizing on noise.
issues.quote: The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced.

issues.description: Participants had to remember dates of past suicidal and mood episodes. Even small date errors can misalign text messages relative to risk states and distort temporal slope analyses.
issues.quote: Participants were generally confident about the accuracy of the dates they selected, rating 90.3% of episodes as ‘very certain’ (i.e., exact days) or ‘somewhat certain’ (i.e., may be off by a few days).

issues.description: When participants had more than three episodes of a type, the manuscript does not specify which were selected. Nonrandom selection of salient, recent, memorable, or data-available episodes can bias comparisons.
issues.quote: For each episode type, we asked about a maximum of three episodes (e.g., three suicide attempts if participant has three or more lifetime attempts).

issues.description: Ideation, depressed, and positive/typical episodes may have occurred at different ages, seasons, relationships, treatment periods, phone ownership periods, or platform-use eras than attempt episodes. Without matching or adjustment, episode-type effects may be confounded by time-varying life circumstances.
issues.quote: participants were asked to identify a number of specific events or episodes in the past and the calendar dates during which the episodes took place.

issues.description: The manuscript does not describe how overlapping or closely spaced episodes were handled. If the same SMS messages contributed to multiple episode types or multiple attempts, independence and classification assumptions would be violated.
issues.quote: A total of 3 to 12 episodes were collected for each participant depending on the presence and number of reported events.

issues.description: The depressed comparison condition also includes high stress, which is not equivalent to depressed mood. Combining depressed mood and high stress may increase heterogeneity and obscure or create differences.
issues.quote: two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt)

issues.description: The manuscript alternates between positive mood and typical mood as the low-risk comparison. These are conceptually different states and may have different language patterns, so the condition definition is unclear.
issues.quote: two-week episode of typical mood (i.e., neither particularly positive nor negative mood and no ideation or attempt).

issues.subcategory: unclear whether language analyses used sent texts only
issues.description: The hypotheses concern participants' language and psychological state, but the methods state that all SMS messages were downloaded and scored. If incoming messages were included in LIWC content analyses, the outcomes partly reflect other people's language, not the participant's state. If they were excluded, this must be clearly reported.
issues.quote: all available SMS data from each device were downloaded (i.e., not from only certain dates or recipients).

issues.subcategory: incoming messages may confound psychological interpretation
issues.description: The manuscript analyzes private text communication but does not clearly separate participant-authored language from correspondents' language for self-focus and sentiment. Constructs like self-focus, anger, and positive emotion have different meanings when expressed by others.
issues.quote: Each individual SMS message was inputted into and scored using the 2015 version of Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)

issues.subcategory: SMS only despite multiple communication channels
issues.description: Participants' interpersonal communication may have occurred through Facebook, Gmail, phone calls, Snapchat, or other platforms. Excluding these channels can produce incomplete and time-varying measurement of communication behavior, especially if platform use changed across episodes.
issues.quote: Additional forms of personal digital data, including phone call history, Google data (Gmail, Hangouts, and Chrome browser history), Facebook messages, and Twitter messages, were collected for the purposes of future analyses but are not part of the current study.

issues.description: Multiple third-party tools and custom cleaning scripts were used, but the manuscript does not report validation against known message counts/content, error rates, duplicate handling, or reproducible code. This threatens data integrity and replicability.
issues.quote: SMS text message data from iPhone and Android phones were accessed using third-party software or phone applications.

issues.description: Collecting SMS from current phones, old phones, laptops, iTunes backups, and cloud sources can create duplicate records. The manuscript does not describe deduplication procedures, which could bias word counts and message volume outcomes.
issues.quote: Participants were asked to bring into the lab as many other devices as they thought might contain digital data (e.g., laptop with iTunes backup, older phone) and all available SMS data from each device were downloaded

issues.description: Historical SMS archives are not necessarily complete because participants may delete conversations or messages, change devices, or lose backups. Selective deletion could correlate with distress, conflict, or suicidality.
issues.quote: Attempts were also made to retrieve data via cloud storage (e.g., iCloud) for messages not available on physical devices (e.g., if a participant had a relatively new phone).

issues.subcategory: LIWC limitations for short SMS language
issues.description: LIWC dictionary counts may perform poorly on short, informal SMS containing abbreviations, slang, misspellings, sarcasm, emojis, images, autocorrect errors, and context-dependent meanings. The manuscript does not validate LIWC categories for this corpus.
issues.quote: LIWC searches a text file and calculates normalized word counts for nearly 6,400 words, word stems, and emoticons that have been previously categorized into a number of linguistic and psychological dimensions.

issues.subcategory: LIWC ignores semantic context and negation
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that single-word LIWC analyses can misclassify meaning, such as treating negated positive emotion as positive. This directly affects sentiment variables central to the main findings.
issues.quote: One weakness of this approach is that examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., “not happy” would count as “positive emotion” because negation is not accounted for)

issues.description: The Tone variable is proprietary and nontransparent, limiting reproducibility and interpretability. Readers cannot know what linguistic features drive the score or whether it is valid for SMS and suicide-risk contexts.
issues.quote: Other LIWC variables include counts of words (e.g., word count of message, words per sentence) and several proprietary, “non-transparent” variables (e.g., Tone)

issues.description: The study treats singular first-person pronoun use as self-focus/rumination, but in SMS this may reflect conversational logistics, narration, relationship context, or recipient prompts rather than maladaptive self-focus. This weakens theoretical interpretation.
issues.quote: we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of rumination) was greater prior to suicide attempts

issues.subcategory: social engagement proxy is overly crude
issues.description: Sent/received ratios and counts are weak proxies for thwarted belongingness, perceived burdensomeness, or social engagement. They do not capture relationship quality, unanswered messages, conflict, support, isolation, or who initiated contact.
issues.quote: decreased social engagement (i.e., lower ratio of sent vs. received text messages).

issues.description: Analyzing 189,478 messages can create a misleadingly large effective sample size when the inferential units for suicide risk are participants and episodes. High-volume texters and long conversations may dominate estimates, and residual dependence among messages can inflate precision.
issues.quote: This approach also allowed us to maximize sources of variance by analyzing on the message level rather than only mean values by episode

issues.subcategory: random slopes omitted in slope models
issues.description: The key temporal analyses require modeling within-person heterogeneity in time and episode-type effects. The planned random slopes did not converge and were removed, which can produce anti-conservative fixed-effect tests and inflated Type I error in repeated-measures designs.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.

issues.subcategory: overly complex model relative to small cluster count
issues.description: The study attempted maximal random-effects models with very few participants and uneven episodes. Such models are likely unstable, prone to convergence problems, and sensitive to modeling choices.
issues.quote: a maximal random effects model, which included random intercepts of participant, episode, and message, and random by-participant slopes, was used

issues.subcategory: unclear or inappropriate random intercept for message
issues.description: A random intercept for message is unusual because each message is generally a unique observation; for aggregated outcomes such as daily counts it is not meaningful unless explicitly used as an observation-level random effect. The manuscript does not clarify the data level for each model sufficiently.
issues.quote: A random by-participant slope for episode type and random intercepts of participant, participant-episode, and message were included as the random effects.

issues.description: GLMM z tests and chi-square tests rely on large-sample approximations. With only about 27 participants contributing SMS data, p-values may be inaccurate, especially for rare word categories and complex random effects.
issues.quote: Any significant tests were followed up with pairwise comparisons between each of the episode types (using z and t statistics for binary/proportion and continuous outcome variables, respectively).

issues.description: The study runs many outcome tests and follow-up pairwise contrasts without multiplicity correction. Several key findings have p-values near .05, making false positives plausible.
issues.quote: Given this is a pilot study with a small and already potentially underpowered sample and the fact that we did not have concrete directional hypotheses for many of the tests, we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction)

issues.description: The authors acknowledge many tests were exploratory and lacked directional hypotheses, yet interpret significant findings as potential risk markers. This increases the risk of HARKing and overinterpretation of chance findings.
issues.quote: Numerous aspects of this research were exploratory by nature.

issues.description: Key claims depend on marginal p-values, including p=.049 and p=.046, without correction for multiple testing or robust validation. These results may not survive even modest adjustment or replication.
issues.quote: positive emotion decreased more steeply during attempt episodes compared to all other episode types, including ideation (z=1.96, p=.049)

issues.description: The analyses test retrospective associations, not classification accuracy. No sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, calibration, cross-validation, or prospective validation is reported, so the study cannot establish that texts identify suicide risk.
issues.quote: We performed inferential analyses using mixed-effects models to examine within-subject (between-episode) differences among suicide attempters in several communication features.

issues.subcategory: linear mixed models for counts and ratios
issues.description: Counts of messages and words are nonnegative, often skewed and overdispersed; ratios can be skewed and bounded or undefined. Treating such outcomes as raw continuous variables in LMMs may violate distributional assumptions.
issues.quote: For outcome variables that were not proportion scores (e.g., number of messages sent per day), the raw continuous variable was used in a linear mixed-effects model (LMM), using the “lmer” function.

issues.description: Sent/received ratios can be undefined when the denominator is zero and unstable when counts are small. The manuscript does not report how zero incoming or outgoing messages were handled.
issues.quote: Ratio sent vs. received messages

issues.description: Rare LIWC categories such as death, sadness, and anger likely produce many zero counts and overdispersion. The manuscript does not report diagnostics, zero-inflated models, negative binomial alternatives, or robustness checks.
issues.quote: For this set of analyses, a significant result says that the odds of a category-specific word appearing in text messages differed as a function of episode type.

issues.description: Modeling category words versus noncategory words as binomial counts assumes a form of independent Bernoulli trials within messages. Words within a message are linguistically dependent, and LIWC categories are contextually clustered, which can bias standard errors without adequate overdispersion handling.
issues.quote: These LIWC percentage scores were converted into counts and then entered as proportions in our models (i.e., number of words in a given text message belonging to versus not belonging to the LIWC category)

issues.description: Messages and daily language patterns are serially correlated within episodes and conversations. The slope models do not report autocorrelation structures, which can bias standard errors and temporal inference.
issues.quote: A series of mixed-effects models were performed for each language feature with 3 fixed effects: episode type (4 levels: attempt, ideation, depressed, positive), day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0), and the interaction of episode type and day.

issues.description: The temporal models assume a linear change across the episode window, despite the authors' own visualizations suggesting variable timing and potentially nonlinear change. Nonlinear trajectories near attempts may be missed or misestimated.
issues.quote: Although highly variable across variables, changes tended to occur most notably and often around 7 days prior to the suicide attempt.

issues.description: For language outcomes, analyses are conditional on messages existing. Days with no texts may themselves indicate social withdrawal or risk, but the content models do not clearly incorporate absent communication as part of the language trajectory.
issues.quote: Each individual SMS message was inputted into and scored using the 2015 version of Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)

issues.description: The models do not appear to adjust for episode recency, participant age at episode, treatment status, diagnosis, relationship context, phone platform, day of week, season, message length, recipient, or substance use. Within-person design helps but does not eliminate time-varying confounding.
issues.quote: A series of mixed-effects models were performed with episode type as a within-subject fixed effect (4 levels: attempt, ideation, depressed, positive) and the language feature of interest as the outcome variable.

issues.description: Mixed models handle missing data under assumptions such as missing at random, but the manuscript implies a general ability to handle missingness. Here, missing SMS data is likely related to device, time, deletion, and episode characteristics.
issues.quote: A mixed-effects method was selected because of its well-established advantages in terms of producing more accurate effect estimates and its ability to handle missing data, non-normal outcome data, and unbalanced classes

issues.description: The power analysis relies on large between-subject effect sizes from different contexts, uses an unclear design effect, and does not account for multiple testing, convergence failures, rare outcomes, or small participant-level clusters. Thus the study's actual power and false-positive risk are uncertain.
issues.quote: We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes (Cramer’s V=0.29)

issues.description: The manuscript reports test statistics and log-odds coefficients but not predicted means/proportions, confidence intervals, or clinically interpretable effect sizes for the main findings. This limits assessment of practical significance.
issues.quote: Here, β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes.

issues.description: The manuscript conflates likelihood-ratio and Wald chi-square tests, which are different inferential procedures. This creates ambiguity about exactly how p-values were obtained.
issues.quote: Likelihood-ratio (Wald chi-square) tests were performed to compare goodness of fit for models including and excluding the fixed effect of episode type.

issues.description: The results text reports p=.003 for the sadness omnibus test, while Table 2 reports .033 for the same chi-square value. This discrepancy affects confidence in reporting accuracy and interpretation.
issues.quote: Regarding sentiment, there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.003.

issues.subcategory: discussion claims anxiety effect not supported
issues.description: The discussion states that attempt periods were associated with greater anxiety and sadness, but the results report no significant anxiety effect. This misstates the findings.
issues.quote: In terms of overall mean differences, few reliable differences emerged though results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness.

issues.description: The text says desire to die decreased from pre to post, but the reported means increase from 0.82 to 1.03 and Table 1 lists a positive change. This indicates a reporting or sign error.
issues.quote: desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=1.03, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033.

issues.description: The manuscript states that 27 participants with SMS data all had data from at least one attempt, but later refers to only 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data. The denominators for attempt analyses are unclear.
issues.quote: Among these 27 participants, all had data from at least one reported suicide attempt.

issues.description: Tables contain duplicated df columns, missing chi-square symbols, and formatting problems. This impairs verification of analyses and may conceal reporting errors.
issues.quote: Self-Focus | Test | df | df | p | β | SE | Test | p

issues.subcategory: risk-state hierarchy assumed rather than measured continuously
issues.description: The study labels entire episode types as high, moderate, or minimal/no risk, but risk likely fluctuates within episodes and depressed or positive/typical periods may still involve concealed or unreported risk. This categorical hierarchy may oversimplify the clinical construct.
issues.quote: attempt episodes were considered “high risk,” ideation episodes were considered “moderate risk,” and depressed and positive episodes were considered “minimal/no risk.”

issues.subcategory: objective assessment claim undermined by self-report labels
issues.description: The manuscript frames the method as avoiding self-report, but the key labels defining high- and low-risk periods are entirely retrospectively self-reported. This undermines the claim of an objective assessment tool.
issues.quote: This approach helps avoid the complications inherent to either patient or clinician self-report

issues.subcategory: nonfatal attempters may differ from suicide decedents
issues.description: The findings may not generalize to suicide deaths or highly lethal attempts. The authors acknowledge attempters and completers can differ, but the title and implications concern suicide risk broadly.
issues.quote: It is possible that characteristics of suicide attempters differ from those of suicide completers

issues.description: Private SMS data include messages written by other people who may not have consented. The manuscript discusses participant data storage but not consent, privacy, or deidentification protections for communication partners, which is important for replicability and ethical evaluation.
issues.quote: all available SMS data from each device were downloaded (i.e., not from only certain dates or recipients).

issues.description: The manuscript notes OSF materials but does not report preregistration of hypotheses, outcomes, exclusion rules, model specifications, or temporal windows. Given many exploratory analyses and researcher degrees of freedom, lack of preregistration weakens evidentiary strength.
issues.quote: Numerous aspects of this research were exploratory by nature.

issues.description: Language and message volume depend heavily on who the participant is texting and the relationship context. Sender/recipient names were removed before analysis, and no model appears to account for conversation partner, which may confound episode differences.
issues.quote: identifying information (e.g., message content, sender/recipient names) were removed prior to analysis.

issues.description: The discussion proposes behind-the-scenes monitoring and notification systems, but the study did not demonstrate predictive accuracy, safety, acceptability, false-positive/false-negative rates, or intervention effectiveness. These implications are premature for the evidence presented.
issues.quote: Knowledge gained from this study could put us one step closer to the development of an objective monitoring tool capable of tracking individuals’ communication “behind the scenes,” notifying suicidal individuals and/or their clinician or family if their patterns of communication indicate increasing levels of suicide risk.
